A.1.name: Nicole Oresme
A.1.alt: Medieval painting of Oresme in a blue robe writing at a wooden desk, beside a large armillary sphere
A.1.caption: Drew changing speed as a shape, and worked out distance from its area, about 250 years before Galileo.
A.1.summary: Nicole Oresme, a teacher in Paris and later a bishop, showed how something that changes, like speed, could be drawn as a shape: a base line for time, with upright lines whose heights show the speed. With this picture he proved that a uniformly accelerating object covers the same distance as one moving steadily at its speed halfway through the time.
A.1.achievements:
• In the 1350s he drew qualities and motions as figures: a base line for the time, with upright lines whose heights showed the speed at each moment. Steady acceleration from rest became a right-angled triangle.
  • He used this picture to give the first proof of the mean speed theorem, found by scholars in Oxford in the 1330s: a uniformly accelerating object goes as far as one moving steadily at its speed halfway through the time. In his figure, the triangle and the rectangle have the same area. This is our idea that the area under a velocity–time graph is the displacement.
  • He never applied it to falling objects. That link came two centuries later.
  • His figures weren't graphs of measured data, but the idea of showing a changing quantity as a shape was a big step towards them.
  • He also wrote on money, astronomy and mathematics, and translated Aristotle into French for King Charles V.
A.1.prompt: Oresme's figures showed imagined speeds, not measurements. Can an idea about motion be useful before anyone can measure it?

A.1.name: Galileo Galilei
A.1.alt: Painted portrait of Galileo as an older man with a grey beard, in dark clothes with a white collar
A.1.caption: Timed balls rolling down ramps to study falling, and showed that a projectile follows a parabola.
A.1.summary: Galileo Galilei rolled balls down gentle ramps to slow falling down enough to time it. He found that distance from rest grows with the square of the time, and showed that a projectile's path is a parabola: steady horizontal motion combined with uniformly accelerated vertical motion.
A.1.achievements:
• Falling is too fast to time by hand, so he rolled balls down gentle slopes. By about 1604 he had found that, starting from rest, the distance travelled is proportional to the square of the time: the sign of uniform acceleration.
  • He treated a projectile's motion as two independent parts: steady horizontal motion and uniformly accelerated vertical motion. Together they give a parabola, just as in section 7.
  • He published this in Two New Sciences (1638). By then the Inquisition had condemned him for supporting the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, and he was under house arrest near Florence, so the book was printed in the Netherlands.
  • The famous story of him dropping balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa comes only from a biography written after his death. It may never have happened.
A.1.prompt: Galileo's results came from slowing a fall down on a ramp. When is it fair to study a slower 'model' of a fast event?

A.2.name: Isaac Newton
A.2.alt: Painted portrait of Newton as a young man with long grey-brown hair, in a dark robe
A.2.caption: Set out three laws of motion that link force and motion for everything from apples to planets.
A.2.summary: Isaac Newton set out the three laws of motion in his book Principia (1687), and used them, with his law of gravitation, to explain both falling objects and the orbits of the planets. His second law was written in terms of change of motion (momentum); the form F = ma came later.
A.2.achievements:
• In Principia (1687) he opened with three “laws of motion”: inertia, the link between force and change of motion, and equal and opposite forces between two bodies.
  • He wrote the second law as change of motion (what we call momentum) being proportional to the force applied. Writing it as F = ma came later, from Euler and others.
  • He built on Galileo's work on motion, and said so himself.
  • He used the same laws, with his law of universal gravitation, to explain both falling objects and the orbits of the planets: one set of rules for Earth and the heavens.
  • He also worked on light and colour, and developed calculus (as Leibniz did, independently).
  • The apple story comes from Newton himself, told when he was old. The apple hitting his head was added later.
A.2.prompt: Newton said he built on the work of others. How much of any scientific discovery belongs to one person?

A.2.name: Emmy Noether
A.2.alt: Old black-and-white photograph of Emmy Noether as a young woman with her hair pinned up
A.2.caption: Proved that conservation of momentum comes from the laws of physics being the same everywhere.
A.2.summary: Emmy Noether, a German mathematician, proved in 1918 that every continuous symmetry in the laws of physics goes with a conserved quantity. Because the laws are the same everywhere, momentum is conserved; because they are the same at all times, energy is conserved. She worked for years unpaid because she was a woman, and was dismissed in 1933 because she was Jewish.
A.2.achievements:
• Noether's theorem (1918) links symmetries to conservation laws. If an experiment works the same when you move it somewhere else, momentum is conserved. If it works the same tomorrow as today, energy is conserved. If it works the same when you turn it round, angular momentum is conserved.
  • So conservation of momentum isn't just a rule found by experiment: it follows from a deep property of space.
  • As a woman she was at first not allowed to hold a university post. At Göttingen her lectures were advertised under David Hilbert's name until she was finally allowed to teach in her own right in 1919.
  • She became one of the founders of modern abstract algebra, and was best known for that in her lifetime.
  • In 1933 the Nazi government dismissed her because she was Jewish. She moved to Bryn Mawr College in the USA and lectured at Princeton, but died in 1935 after an operation.
A.2.prompt: Noether was kept out of paid university posts for years because she was a woman. What does science lose when people are shut out of it?

A.3.name: James Prescott Joule
A.3.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Joule as an older man with a grey beard, sitting in a dark suit
A.3.caption: Showed that work done stirring water always produces the same amount of heating: energy is conserved.
A.3.summary: James Joule, from a family of brewers in Salford, used falling weights to turn paddles in water and measured the tiny rise in temperature. The same amount of work always gave the same heating, which helped to establish conservation of energy. The SI unit of energy is named after him.
A.3.achievements:
• In his paddle-wheel experiment, falling weights turned paddles that stirred water. The friction warmed the water by a fraction of a degree, and he measured it with very precise thermometers.
  • He found that the same amount of mechanical work always produced the same amount of heating: the “mechanical equivalent of heat”. His value improved over years of repeats, from 1845 to 1850.
  • This was key evidence that heat is a form of energy and that energy is conserved, not used up.
  • He wasn't a university professor: he helped run his family's brewery and did his research privately, with careful measurement learned partly from the chemist John Dalton.
  • He worked with William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin) on how gases cool when they expand.
  • On his honeymoon in the Alps he carried a thermometer, hoping to show that water is warmer at the bottom of a waterfall than at the top. The falls were too broken by spray to measure.
  • The SI unit of energy, the joule, is named after him.
A.3.prompt: Joule's temperature rises were less than a degree. Why did such small measurements convince other scientists?

A.3.name: Émilie du Châtelet
A.3.alt: Painted portrait of du Châtelet, a woman in an 18th-century dress, holding a pair of dividers
A.3.caption: Argued that the “force” of a moving object depends on v², the idea behind kinetic energy.
A.3.summary: Émilie du Châtelet, a French mathematician and physicist, argued in her book Foundations of Physics (1740) that what a moving object can do depends on mv², not mv. She used experiments in which balls dropped into soft clay made dents that depended on the square of their speed. Her French translation of Newton's Principia is still used today.
A.3.achievements:
• In the early 1700s scientists argued about how to measure the “force” of a moving object: mv (what we now call momentum) or mv² (which Leibniz called vis viva, “living force”).
  • In her book Institutions de physique (Foundations of Physics, 1740) she argued strongly for mv². Her evidence came from experiments by the Dutch scientist Willem 's Gravesande: balls dropped into soft clay made dents whose size depended on mv². This is the idea behind kinetic energy. The ½ in ½mv² was added about 90 years later.
  • She entered the Paris Academy's 1738 prize essay on the nature of fire, in secret. She didn't win, but the Academy published her essay alongside the winners.
  • She translated Newton's Principia into French, with her own commentary, finishing just before her death. It is still the standard French translation.
  • Women couldn't join the Academy of Sciences, so she learned from tutors and corresponded with leading scientists.
A.3.prompt: Scientists argued for decades about whether mv or mv² was the 'real' force of motion. Both turned out to be useful. Can two rival ideas both be right?

A.4.name: Archimedes
A.4.origin: Syracuse, a Greek city in Sicily
A.4.alt: Painting of Archimedes as an old bearded man leaning on a table, deep in thought, with a globe, books and drawing instruments
A.4.caption: Proved the law of the lever, the first form of the idea of torque.
A.4.summary: Archimedes of Syracuse proved the law of the lever: two weights balance when their distances from the pivot are in inverse proportion to their weights. In today's words, the clockwise and anticlockwise torques are equal. He also found the centres of gravity of shapes such as triangles. (The painting was made about 1800 years after his death, so nobody knows what he really looked like.)
A.4.achievements:
• In On the Equilibrium of Planes he proved the law of the lever: weights balance when their distances from the pivot are inversely proportional to the weights. That is our condition that the torques balance, F1d1 = F2d2.
  • He found the centres of gravity of a triangle, a parallelogram and other shapes using geometry.
  • He also discovered the principle of buoyancy (see A.2) and found remarkably accurate values for π.
  • “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth” is a boast later writers put into his mouth, centuries after his death.
  • He was killed in 212 BC when the Romans captured Syracuse.
A.4.prompt: Archimedes proved the lever law from geometry, not from experiments. Is a proof stronger evidence than a measurement?

A.4.name: Al-Khazini
A.4.alt: Page from a 13th-century Arabic manuscript showing a long balance beam with hanging pans, drawn in red and black ink
A.4.caption: Wrote The Book of the Balance of Wisdom (1121), on centres of gravity and precision balances.
A.4.summary: Al-Khazini was born in the Byzantine Empire and brought as a slave to Merv, in Central Asia, where his owner gave him a scholar's education. In 1121 he wrote The Book of the Balance of Wisdom, which gathered what was known about centres of gravity, levers and balances, and described a balance precise enough to tell pure metals from fakes. No portrait of him survives: the picture shows his balance in a copy of the book made about 150 years later.
A.4.achievements:
• He was born in the Byzantine Empire and taken as a slave to Merv, a great city of the Seljuk empire in Central Asia. His owner, a treasury official, gave him an excellent education.
  • His Kitab Mizan al-Hikma (The Book of the Balance of Wisdom, 1121) brought together centuries of work by Greek and Islamic scholars, including Archimedes, Ibn al-Haytham and al-Biruni, on centres of gravity, levers and balances.
  • Its centrepiece was his “balance of wisdom”, a very precise balance that could also weigh objects in water. Comparing the two readings gave a material's density, so it could tell pure gold from an alloy.
  • The book lists the densities of many metals, gems and liquids, building on careful measurements by al-Biruni a century earlier.
  • He also thought about how weight might change with distance from the Earth's centre, though his idea was very different from Newton's later law.
  • He also wrote astronomical tables for the sultan Sanjar.
A.4.prompt: Al-Khazini's book collected and checked the work of many earlier scholars. How important is gathering and testing others' work, compared with making new discoveries?

A.5.name: Hendrik Lorentz
A.5.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Lorentz, an older man with a white beard and moustache, in a suit
A.5.caption: Worked out the transformation equations of relativity before Einstein gave them their meaning.
A.5.summary: Hendrik Lorentz, a Dutch theoretical physicist, worked out the equations that connect measurements made in frames moving relative to each other, now called the Lorentz transformations. He thought they described real effects of moving through an 'ether'; Einstein showed in 1905 that they follow from the nature of space and time. Lorentz won the 1902 Nobel Prize for explaining how magnetism splits spectral lines.
A.5.achievements:
• Between about 1892 and 1904 he built up the equations that link positions and times measured in two frames moving relative to each other. In 1905 Henri Poincaré named them the Lorentz transformations.
  • Like the Irish physicist George FitzGerald, he independently suggested that moving objects contract along their direction of motion, to explain why experiments couldn't detect the Earth moving through the “ether”.
  • He thought the contraction was a real physical squeezing caused by the ether. Einstein's 1905 theory used the same equations but without any ether, as a property of space and time themselves.
  • He shared the 1902 Nobel Prize with his former student Pieter Zeeman, for explaining how a magnetic field splits spectral lines (the Zeeman effect), not for relativity.
  • Einstein admired him enormously and spoke at his funeral in 1928.
A.5.prompt: Lorentz and Einstein used the same equations but explained them in completely different ways. If two theories make the same predictions, how do we choose between them?

A.5.name: Albert Einstein
A.5.origin: Germany; later Switzerland and the USA
A.5.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Einstein as an older man with white hair and a moustache
A.5.caption: Built special relativity on two postulates, while working as a clerk in a patent office.
A.5.summary: Albert Einstein, working as a clerk in the Swiss patent office in Bern, published special relativity in 1905. He started from two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and the speed of light in a vacuum is the same whatever the motion of its source. Time dilation, length contraction and the relativity of simultaneity all follow.
A.5.achievements:
• In 1905 he was a technical expert at the patent office in Bern, Switzerland, doing physics in his spare time.
  • That year his paper “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies” set out special relativity from two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, and light in a vacuum travels at the same speed c whatever the motion of its source.
  • Others, including Lorentz and Poincaré, already had much of the mathematics. Einstein's new step was to drop the ether and accept what the postulates say about time and simultaneity.
  • In 1915 he extended his ideas to gravity in general relativity.
  • His 1921 Nobel Prize was for explaining the photoelectric effect (HL topic E.2), not for relativity.
  • He left Germany at the end of 1932 and never went back after the Nazis came to power. He worked at Princeton in the USA for the rest of his life.
  • The story that he failed maths at school is a myth.
A.5.prompt: Einstein made his breakthrough outside a university, in his spare time. Does it matter where new ideas come from?

B.1.name: Joseph Black
B.1.alt: Engraved portrait of Joseph Black, an older man with white hair, sitting in an armchair in a dark coat
B.1.caption: Discovered latent heat, and that different materials need different amounts of heat to warm up.
B.1.summary: Joseph Black, a chemistry professor in Glasgow and Edinburgh, noticed that melting ice takes in heat without getting any warmer. He called this hidden heat “latent heat”, and measured it for melting ice and for boiling water. He also found that equal masses of different substances need different amounts of heat for the same temperature rise: the idea of specific heat capacity.
B.1.achievements:
• Around 1761 he showed that ice at its melting point takes in a lot of heat while it melts, with no rise in temperature. He called it latent (hidden) heat, and the next year he measured the latent heat of steam too.
  • He also found that equal masses of different substances need different amounts of heat for the same temperature rise. This is specific heat capacity, which he called the “capacity for heat”.
  • He was a professor of chemistry at Glasgow and then at Edinburgh, and he was also a doctor. He discovered carbon dioxide, which he called “fixed air”.
  • He never published his work on heat: students learned it from his lectures, which were printed after his death.
  • James Watt, the steam-engine inventor, was his friend at Glasgow, and they discussed latent heat. How much Black's ideas shaped Watt's improved engine is still debated.
B.1.prompt: Black never published his discoveries about heat; people learned them from his lectures. Does knowledge count as scientific if it's never published?

B.1.name: Mária Telkes
B.1.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Mária Telkes, a smiling woman with short wavy hair, wearing a white lab coat

credit.author: New York World-Telegram and the Sun staff photographer (1956)

B.1.caption: Stored the Sun's energy as latent heat in melting salt, to heat a house through the winter.
B.1.summary: Mária Telkes, a Hungarian-American scientist nicknamed the “Sun Queen”, designed the heating for the Dover Sun House (1948). Sunlight warmed air that melted tonnes of a salt in the walls; when the salt froze again it gave back its latent heat to keep the house warm on cloudy days. She also invented a solar still that turned seawater into drinking water for people adrift in life rafts.
B.1.achievements:
• She trained as a physical chemist in Budapest and moved to the USA in 1925, becoming a US citizen in 1937.
  • In the Second World War she designed a small solar still that used sunlight to turn seawater into drinking water (up to about a litre a day). It went into the emergency kits on life rafts.
  • In 1948 she designed the heating for the Dover Sun House in Massachusetts, with the architect Eleanor Raymond. It was paid for by the sculptor Amelia Peabody: a project led by three women.
  • Sunlight heated air behind glass, and the warm air melted about 21 tonnes of Glauber's salt stored in the walls. The salt melts at about 32 °C, so it stored the energy as latent heat and released it when it froze again.
  • The system heated the house for about two winters, then failed: the salt separated into layers and the containers leaked. Storing heat in phase-change materials is now a growing technology.
  • She held about 20 patents, including solar ovens, and was nicknamed the “Sun Queen”.
B.1.prompt: Telkes's sun-heated house worked for two winters, then failed. Was it a success or a failure, and what can scientists learn from a design that breaks?

B.2.name: Eunice Newton Foote
B.2.alt: Printed page of Eunice Foote's 1856 paper “Circumstances affecting the heat of the Sun's rays”, with tables of temperatures in shade and in sun

credit.author: American Journal of Science and Arts (1856)

B.2.caption: In 1856 showed that carbon dioxide warms more in sunlight than ordinary air, and suggested it could warm the Earth.
B.2.summary: Eunice Newton Foote put thermometers in glass cylinders of different gases and left them in sunlight. The cylinder of carbon dioxide got hottest and stayed hot longest, and she suggested that more of this gas in the air would make the Earth warmer. Her paper was read at a science meeting in 1856, by a male scientist rather than by her. No portrait of her is known: the picture is the page where her results were published.
B.2.achievements:
• She filled glass cylinders with different gases (moist and dry air, carbon dioxide, hydrogen, oxygen), each with a thermometer, and put them in sunlight. The carbon dioxide cylinder warmed most, to about 52 °C, and cooled most slowly.
  • She concluded that an atmosphere with more of this gas would give the Earth a higher temperature: one of the first suggestions of a link between carbon dioxide and climate.
  • Her paper was read at the American Association for the Advancement of Science meeting in 1856 by the physicist Joseph Henry, not by her, and then published under her name.
  • Her experiment used sunlight, not the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth, so it couldn't show how greenhouse gases work. John Tyndall measured how gases absorb infrared in 1859, and the two are now seen as pioneers.
  • In 1848 she signed the Declaration of Sentiments at the Seneca Falls Convention, the start of the women's rights movement in the USA.
  • Her work was almost forgotten until 2010–11, when researchers rediscovered it.
  • No portrait of her is known, so the picture shows the page where her results were published.
B.2.prompt: Foote's result was forgotten for about 150 years. Why might some scientists' work be overlooked, and how could that change what we think we know about the history of science?

B.2.name: Syukuro Manabe
B.2.alt: Photograph of Syukuro Manabe, a smiling older man with grey hair and glasses, wearing a dark jacket and red tie

credit.author: Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (Japan)

B.2.caption: Built the first realistic computer models of climate, and won the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics.
B.2.summary: Syukuro Manabe moved from Japan to the USA in 1958 to build computer models of the atmosphere. In 1967 he and Richard Wetherald showed with a model that doubling the carbon dioxide in the air would warm the Earth's surface by about 2 °C. He shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics for modelling Earth's climate.
B.2.achievements:
• Born in a village in Ehime, Japan, he studied in Tokyo and moved to the USA in 1958 to build computer models of the atmosphere for the US Weather Bureau.
  • In 1967, with Richard Wetherald, he built a model that included how warm air rises (convection) and how a warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour. It showed that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the surface by about 2 °C, and that the upper atmosphere would cool.
  • Others had estimated the warming before, but his was the first physically realistic model, and later results have agreed with it remarkably well.
  • In 1969, with Kirk Bryan, he linked a model of the atmosphere to a model of the ocean for the first time.
  • In 2021 he shared half of the Nobel Prize in Physics with Klaus Hasselmann “for the physical modelling of Earth's climate, quantifying variability and reliably predicting global warming”.
B.2.prompt: Manabe's 1967 prediction was made with a simple model and early computers, yet it has held up for over 50 years. What makes us trust a model's prediction about the future?

B.3.name: Robert Boyle
B.3.alt: Painted portrait of Robert Boyle, a man with long curly hair and a white neck-cloth, seated beside a table with a book
B.3.caption: Showed with a J-shaped tube of mercury that a gas's pressure and volume are inversely proportional.
B.3.summary: Robert Boyle, born in Ireland, trapped air in the short sealed end of a J-shaped glass tube and poured mercury into the long end. Doubling the pressure halved the volume of the trapped air: pressure and volume are inversely proportional. He published this in 1662, and it's now called Boyle's law.
B.3.achievements:
• With his assistant Robert Hooke, who designed and built their air pump, he did many experiments on the “spring of the air”: how air pushes back when it is squeezed.
  • In a J-shaped tube, he trapped air in the short sealed end and added mercury to the long open end. Doubling the pressure on the air halved its volume.
  • He published the rule that pressure and volume are inversely proportional in 1662. He credited Richard Towneley with suggesting it from the data; Boyle's careful experiments established it.
  • He didn't say the temperature had to stay constant. The French scientist Edme Mariotte found the same law independently in the 1670s and added that condition; in France it's called Mariotte's law.
  • He was a founding member of the Royal Society (1660) and insisted that experiments be described in enough detail for others to repeat them.
B.3.prompt: Boyle's law is named after Boyle, but Hooke built the pump, Towneley suggested the rule and Mariotte found it independently. Who deserves the credit for a scientific law?

B.3.name: Daniel Bernoulli
B.3.alt: Engraved portrait of Daniel Bernoulli in a curled wig and embroidered coat, inside an ornate frame with a Latin inscription

credit.author: Johann Jakob Haid after Johann Rudolf Huber

B.3.caption: First explained gas pressure as tiny particles hitting the walls, over a century before anyone took it seriously.
B.3.summary: Daniel Bernoulli, from a famous Swiss family of mathematicians, suggested in 1738 that a gas is made of tiny particles moving fast in all directions, and that its pressure comes from them hitting the walls. From this picture he derived Boyle's law. His idea was largely ignored for over a century, until the kinetic theory of gases was developed in the 1850s.
B.3.achievements:
• In his book Hydrodynamica (1738) he pictured a gas as huge numbers of tiny particles moving rapidly, with the pressure caused by their collisions with the walls, just as in section 6.
  • From this model he derived Boyle's law, and showed that the pressure depends on the square of the particles' speed.
  • Almost nobody followed it up for over a century. Others rediscovered the idea, and Joule, Clausius and Maxwell finally built the kinetic theory of gases in the 1850s.
  • The same book links the pressure in a moving fluid to its speed: Bernoulli's principle, used to explain how fluids flow. The equation in today's form was written later, by Leonhard Euler.
  • His father Johann and uncle Jacob were famous mathematicians too. His father competed with him bitterly, and even back-dated one of his own books to claim earlier credit.
B.3.prompt: Bernoulli's particle model of a gas was ignored for over a century. Why might a correct idea not be accepted when it is first proposed?

B.4.name: Sadi Carnot
B.4.alt: Drawing of the young Sadi Carnot with dark wavy hair, wearing a high-collared military-style jacket with buttons
B.4.caption: Showed that the best possible efficiency of a heat engine depends only on two temperatures.
B.4.summary: Sadi Carnot, a young French army engineer, asked how much work a steam engine could possibly get from heat. In his only book (1824) he described an ideal reversible engine cycle, and showed that no engine working between the same two temperatures can do better, whatever its working substance. The Carnot cycle is the basis of the second law of thermodynamics.
B.4.achievements:
• In 1824, aged 28, he published Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, his only book, asking what limits the work a steam engine can get from heat.
  • He imagined an ideal, reversible engine: the Carnot cycle. He showed that no engine working between the same hot and cold temperatures can do better, and that the best possible efficiency depends only on those two temperatures, not on whether the engine uses steam, air or anything else.
  • He reasoned with the old “caloric” theory, picturing heat as a fluid flowing from hot to cold like water through a water wheel. His private notes show he was moving towards the idea that heat is a form of motion.
  • The formula η = 1 − Tc/Th came later, when Kelvin and Clausius combined his ideas with conservation of energy.
  • His book was almost ignored. He died of cholera in 1832, aged 36, and his work became famous only after Clapeyron, Kelvin and Clausius took it up.
B.4.prompt: Carnot reached a correct conclusion using a theory of heat (caloric) that was wrong. How can a wrong theory lead to a right result?

B.4.name: Ludwig Boltzmann
B.4.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Ludwig Boltzmann, a man with a long dark beard and round glasses, above his signature
B.4.caption: Explained entropy by counting the ways the particles of a system can be arranged.
B.4.summary: Ludwig Boltzmann, an Austrian physicist, explained entropy using atoms and probability: a state with more possible arrangements of its particles (microstates) has more entropy, so systems naturally move towards it. The equation S = k log W is carved on his grave in Vienna, and the Boltzmann constant k is named after him.
B.4.achievements:
• In 1872 and 1877 he linked entropy to probability: entropy depends on the number of ways (microstates) the particles of a system can be arranged and still look the same from outside.
  • This explains why entropy increases: there are far more disordered arrangements than ordered ones, so a system is overwhelmingly likely to move towards disorder.
  • The equation S = k log W is carved above his bust on his grave in Vienna. In fact Max Planck first wrote it in that form and introduced the constant k, which he named after Boltzmann.
  • Many leading scientists of his time, such as Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, doubted that atoms were real, and he had to defend his ideas for years. Experiments by Jean Perrin, explained by Einstein, convinced most scientists soon after his death.
  • He suffered from depression and poor health for many years, and he died in 1906.
B.4.prompt: Boltzmann built his theory on atoms when many scientists doubted they existed. How much evidence should scientists need before accepting something they can't see?

B.5.name: Lewis Latimer
B.5.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Lewis Latimer as a young man with glasses and a moustache, in a jacket and patterned cravat
B.5.caption: Patented a better way to make the carbon filaments that glowed inside early electric lamps.
B.5.summary: Lewis Latimer was the son of George and Rebecca Latimer, who had escaped slavery. He taught himself technical drawing and became an inventor and expert on electric lighting. In 1882 he patented a better way to make carbon filaments, the thin high-resistance threads that glow white-hot in a filament lamp, and in 1890 he wrote a book on electric lighting.
B.5.achievements:
• His parents escaped slavery in Virginia in 1842. When his father was arrested in Boston, a huge campaign bought his freedom and led to a Massachusetts law against helping to capture people who had escaped slavery.
  • At 16 he joined the US Navy in the Civil War. Afterwards he worked as an office boy at a patent firm, taught himself mechanical drawing, and became its draftsman. (He later said he drew the patent drawings for Alexander Graham Bell's telephone, but no record has been found to confirm it.)
  • Working for Hiram Maxim's electric lighting company, a rival of Edison's, he patented in 1882 a better way to make carbon filaments: baking them inside a cardboard envelope so they didn't warp or break. A filament needs a high resistance so that the current heats it until it glows.
  • In 1882 he went to London to help set up a lamp factory.
  • He later worked for Edison's company as a patent expert and in 1890 wrote one of the first books on electric lighting. He was a founding member of the Edison Pioneers.
  • He also wrote poetry, painted, and taught drawing to immigrants in New York.
B.5.prompt: Latimer taught himself technical drawing while working as an office boy. What barriers stop talented people becoming scientists or engineers, then and now?

B.5.name: Georg Simon Ohm
B.5.alt: Black-and-white portrait of Georg Simon Ohm, an older man with curly grey hair, in a dark coat with a medal at his collar
B.5.caption: Measured how current depends on wire length, finding the law that now carries his name.
B.5.summary: Georg Simon Ohm, a German school teacher, measured the current through wires of different lengths using a steady thermocouple as his source. In 1827 he published the result now called Ohm's law: for a conductor at constant temperature, the current is proportional to the potential difference. At first his work was poorly received, but later he was honoured, and the unit of resistance, the ohm, is named after him.
B.5.achievements:
• Early batteries gave a current that kept changing, so he used a thermocouple instead: two different metals joined, with one junction in ice and the other in boiling water, which gave a steady emf.
  • He measured the current through wires of different lengths with a sensitive magnetic needle hung on a twisting wire.
  • In 1827 he published the result in his book The Galvanic Circuit Investigated Mathematically: the current is proportional to the driving voltage divided by the resistance of the circuit. In today's form, V = IR with R constant at constant temperature.
  • The book got a cool reception in Germany, where it was thought too mathematical. He had hoped for a university post, gave up his teaching job, and struggled for years.
  • Recognition came from abroad: Britain's Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal in 1841. He became a professor in Munich only two years before he died.
  • The unit of resistance was named the ohm in the 1860s.
